title: Berkshire 1994 letter: intrinsic value, capital allocation, aligned pay and the USAir mistake
summary: Buffett's 1994 letter explains intrinsic value vs book value using Scott Fetzer, warns against dilution-focused acquisitions, and lays out symmetric manager compensation. It also covers insurance float, pricing rather than timing purchases, ignoring forecasts, and owning up to the USAir error.

principles.text: Intrinsic value, not book value, is what counts: discounted cash that can be taken out of a business over its life.
principles.quote: We define intrinsic value as the discounted value of the cash that can be taken out of a business during its remaining life.

principles.text: Ignore macro forecasts; fear of unknowns shouldn't delay buying good businesses at sensible prices.
principles.quote: Fear is the foe of the faddist, but the friend of the fundamentalist.

principles.text: Price purchases rather than time them; don't scrap an informed decision over uninformed guesses.
principles.quote: We try to price, rather than time, purchases. In our view, it is folly to forego buying shares in an outstanding business whose long-term future is predictable, because of short-term worries about an economy or a stock market that we know to be unpredictable.

principles.text: Judge acquisitions by per-share intrinsic value, not near-term EPS dilution; most deals enrich the target and the bankers, not the acquirer's owners.
principles.quote: That happens because the acquirer typically gives up more intrinsic value than it receives.

principles.text: Real alignment means sharing downside as well as upside; charge managers for capital and credit them for releasing it.
principles.quote: In our book, alignment means being a partner in both directions, not just on the upside.

principles.text: Insurance float is valuable only if its cost is below the market cost of money; accept lumpy results rather than smoothing earnings.
principles.quote: An insurance business is profitable over time if its cost of float is less than the cost the company would otherwise incur to obtain funds.
